Wishing for solutions doesn't make it so. The research in to living off planet will take as long as it takes, and trying to put arbitrary release dates on solutions to complex problems simply doesn't work. Many people seem to think more money and manpower is all it takes to speed these things up. If you double the money and the manpower, that a breakthrough should take half the time. The real world often doesn't work this way.

The problem isn't technology to survive the journey, it's our unwillingness to build the infrastructure to do so. There are simple low tech solutions to deep space living, but none of them can be implemented in gravity well and then launched straight to Mars. We need a craft built for vacuum and in vacuum. That's the only feasible way to provide spin gravity to fight bone density loss and create a craft with an outer water shield thick enough to prevent radiation exposure.

I'm not saying it can't be done. I'm saying stop assigning arbitrary completion dates to complex problems. It doesn't work. This idea that science must come up with a fully working solution in X years or get mothballed is an attitude we need to leave behind if we intend to get off this rock in any permanent fashion.

Politicians need to stop treating NASA like it's hedging a political bet where NASA can make them look good via landmark accomplishments occurring inside of their term. They need to start believing that it's a truly necessary thing for our species. I don't think any of them have really believed in space travel since the JFK administration, and if it's going to work the plan has to be long term and not easy to dismantle by the next administration in line.
Politicians are reliably out of touch. They think they can just "make it so" through legislation without really understanding the problems and complexity.

I suppose you're correct about the 'mothball' attitude, though I also think that isn't what most people take issue with. It is more the attitude presented by the Planetary Society, that a current mission to Mars would be suicidal and that the only path forward is to pump tons of money into basic science.

It seems to me that rather than more basic science we need engineering work done to create a highway up the gravity well, as well as an extra Planetary supply chain. There is no reason why we need to even bring all of the materials for a project like this up from earth. There are plenty of resource rich asteroids we could use for the raw materials instead. And you see some of this being done by guys like Soon Musk with the dragon heavy project. As well as even NASA talking about capturing an asteroid in the 2020s (albeit for research not resource harvest). That being said, there is no good excuse for not populating at least the Van Allen Belt in preparation for the supply and manufacturing chain needed to undertake populating Mars.

As for your statement about politicians needing to see the benefit and necessity of an outside earth population, I agree completely, though I hope that pioneers like Soon Musk are setting things up such that politicians need not play a part in this in the near future. I'm more interested in engaging people and then giving them the training and physical prep needed to be useful in a post-earth society. With enough of them we won't need anybody else, we can simply go ourselves.
